title: Capstone
objectives: I can explain why the new words of this unit, such as 'носі́й мо́ви', 'вдоскона́лювати' and 'впе́внений', are spelled and said as they are, with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress.
I can read and tell a longer story about my own progress, choosing the case of each noun, the aspect of each verb and the right verb of motion.
I can join ideas in complex sentences with 'щоб', 'якби́', relative clauses and adverbial participles, and say the same thing in the simpler way of conversation.
I can move from 'ти' among friends to 'ви' and to a formal letter, and address each person with the right form of the name.
I can talk about my pronunciation, my vocabulary and my plans, defend my view of how to keep learning, and thank people and wish them success.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'прогре́су', with the '-у' that abstract nouns usually take. Progress in something takes 'у' with the locative: 'прогре́с у вимо́ві', progress in pronunciation.

example.source: Sam, I can see your progress.

vocabulary.note: 'Носі́й' is made from 'носи́ти', to carry, and names a person who carries something; 'мо́ви' is the genitive of 'мо́ва'. A native speaker is someone who has spoken the language since childhood. Only 'носі́й' declines: 'носія́ мо́ви', plural 'носії́ мо́ви', 'з носія́ми мо́ви'. The phrase is used for a woman as well as for a man.

example.target: Сем ча́сто гово́рить із носія́ми мо́ви.
example.source: Sam often talks with native speakers.
example.source_literal: Sam often speaks with carriers of-language.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'акце́нту'. It is the foreign accent of a speaker: 'говори́ти з акце́нтом', to speak with an accent; 'без акце́нту', without an accent. It does not mean the stress of a word.

example.target: Сем гово́рить украї́нською з акце́нтом, але́ його́ всі розумі́ють.
example.source: Sam speaks Ukrainian with an accent, but everyone understands him.
example.source_literal: Sam speaks by-Ukrainian with accent, but him all understand.

vocabulary.note: Built from the prefix 'ви-', out, and the root of 'мо́ва': the way words come out in speech. The verb is 'вимовля́ти', to pronounce, with the perfective 'ви́мовити'.

Genitive 'словника́', locative 'у словнику́'. Made from 'сло́во' and the suffix '-ник': a book or an app of words, and also all the words a person knows: 'У Се́ма вели́кий словни́к.', Sam has a large vocabulary.

example.source: I already read without a dictionary.

vocabulary.note: Genitive 'сти́лю', with a soft 'ль' and the ending '-ю'. The style of a letter is formal to an official or a teacher and friendly to a friend.

example.source: Every letter has its own style.

vocabulary.note: The adjective of 'мо́ва'. Where English puts the noun 'language' before another noun, Ukrainian uses this adjective, which agrees with the noun: 'мо́вна шко́ла', a language school; 'мо́вні поми́лки', language mistakes.

example.source: There are many language schools in Kyiv.

vocabulary.note: 'Вдоскона́люю', 'вдоскона́люєш'. Perfective partner 'вдоскона́лити' ('вдоскона́лю', 'вдоскона́лиш'). It is built on 'доскона́лий', perfect, flawless, and is used for a skill or a thing one works on over time. After a word that ends in a consonant it is written with 'у': 'Сем удоскона́лює вимо́ву.'

example.source: I work on my Ukrainian every day.

vocabulary.note: 'Впе́внена', 'впе́внене', 'впе́внені'. With 'що' and a clause it means sure that something is true; 'впе́внений у собі́' means self-confident, literally 'sure in oneself'. It has the form of a passive participle of 'впе́внити', to convince, but it is used as an ordinary adjective. After a word that ends in a consonant it is written with 'у': 'Він упе́внений.'

example.target: Окса́на впе́внена, що Сем пове́рнеться до Ки́єва.
example.source: Oksana is sure that Sam will come back to Kyiv.
example.source_literal: Oksana sure, that Sam will-return to Kyiv.

vocabulary.note: The adverb of 'ві́льний', free. With a language it means fluently: 'ві́льно говори́ти украї́нською'.
Genitive 'пі́дсумку': the 'о' drops when an ending is added, as in 'раху́нок', 'раху́нку'. 'У пі́дсумку' means 'in the end, all things considered', and often opens the last paragraph of an essay.

example.source: Here is a short summary of our conversation.

vocabulary.part_of_speech: neuter noun, declined like an adjective
vocabulary.note: The neuter of the adjective 'майбу́тній', future, used as a noun for what is to come. Because it began as an adjective, it keeps the soft adjective endings: 'про майбу́тнє', 'у майбу́тньому', in the future.

example.target: У майбу́тньому я хо́чу працюва́ти в Украї́ні.
example.source: In the future I want to work in Ukraine.
example.source_literal: In future I want to-work in Ukraine.

vocabulary.note: From the root of 'дя́кувати', to thank. 'Ви́словити по́дяку' with the dative of the person is to express one's thanks, a phrase of speeches and letters; in conversation people simply say 'дя́кую'.

example.target: Сем ви́словив по́дяку всім свої́м дру́зям.
example.source_literal: Sam expressed gratitude to-all to-own to-friends.

vocabulary.note: The adverb of 'щи́рий', sincere, warm-hearted. 'Щи́ро дя́кую' is a warmer thank-you than 'дя́кую' alone, in speech and in letters.

example.source: Thank you sincerely for the advice.

vocabulary.source: good luck, I wish you success
vocabulary.note: 'Бажа́ти' takes the person in the dative and the thing wished in the genitive: 'Бажа́ю тобі́ у́спіхів.', 'Бажа́ю вам у́спіхів.' 'У́спіх' is success, and 'у́спіхів' is its genitive plural. People say it before an exam, a new job or a journey, and at the end of a letter.

dialogues.title: A farewell evening at Andrii's café
dialogues.context: On Sam's last Friday in Kyiv his friends gather at Andrii's café; on Sunday he flies home to Canada. Sam, Oksana and Taras are friends and say 'ти' to one another. They and Andrii say 'ви' to each other, as the café owner and his regular customers always have, and Sam calls him 'па́не Андрі́ю'. 'Сумува́ти за' with the instrumental means to miss someone: 'Я бу́ду сумува́ти за ва́ми.', 'I will miss you.' A toast begins with 'за' and the accusative: 'За Се́ма!', 'To Sam!'

lines.target: До́брий ве́чір усі́м! Се́ме, ка́ва сього́дні від ме́не, як пода́рунок.
lines.source: Good evening, everyone! Sam, the coffee's on me tonight, as a present.
lines.source_literal: Good evening to-all! Sam, coffee today from me, as present.

dialogues.title: What to study next
dialogues.context: After his last class Sam stays behind to ask his teacher, Iryna Petrivna, how to keep up his Ukrainian in Canada. Teacher and student say 'ви' to each other. 'Повто́рювати за' with the instrumental is to repeat after someone. «Лісова́ пі́сня», 'The Forest Song', is a play in verse by Lesia Ukrainka.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна
lines.target: О́тже, Се́ме, ви хоті́ли поговори́ти про те, що вивча́ти да́лі?

lines.source_literal: Yes, Iryna Petrivna. On Sunday I fly to Canada and fear to-forget Ukrainian.

lines.speaker: Іри́на Петрі́вна

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: носі́й мо́ви, вдоскона́лювати, впе́внений and the other new words
grammar.explanation:
Every new word of this unit can be read with the rules of the alphabet units and the unit on stress, and none needs a new rule. The points below are the ones that are easy to miss.

'Носі́й' [nɔˈsʲij] has two syllables, 'но-сі́й'. The 'й' after 'і' is the consonant [j], not a vowel, so it adds no syllable, and the 'с' is soft before 'і'. The word is the stem of 'носи́ти', to carry, with the suffix '-ій', which names a person who does something. In its other forms the ending begins with a vowel, and the [j] is written inside the vowel letter after 'і', as in 'бою́ся': 'носія́' [nɔsʲiˈjɑ], 'носіє́м', plural 'носії́' [nɔsʲiˈji], 'носії́в', 'з носія́ми'. In all of them the stress moves to the ending. In 'носі́й мо́ви' only 'носі́й' changes, because 'мо́ви' is a genitive that belongs to it: 'з носія́ми мо́ви'.

'Вдоскона́лювати' [wdɔskɔˈnɑlʲuʋɑtɪ] has six syllables, 'вдо-ско-на́-лю-ва-ти'. Its first 'в' stands before the consonant 'д', so it is said [w], as in 'вдо́ма'. After a word that ends in a consonant it is written 'у', by the euphony rule of the unit on stress, which keeps vowels and consonants alternating: 'Я вдоскона́люю вимо́ву.' but 'Сем удоскона́лює вимо́ву.' The verb is built on 'доскона́лий', perfect, with the prefix 'в-' and the suffix '-юва-', the form '-ува-' takes after a soft consonant: the 'л' is soft before 'ю'. In the present '-юва-' becomes '-ю-', as '-ува-' becomes '-у-' in every such verb, and in this verb the stress stays on 'на́' in every form: 'вдоскона́люю', 'вдоскона́люєш', 'вдоскона́люють'. In 'вдоскона́люю' the first 'ю' softens the 'л', and the second, after a vowel, is [ju].

'Впе́внений' [ˈwpɛwnɛnɪj] has two letters 'в', and each stands before a consonant, so both are [w]: 'впе́в-не-ний'. After a consonant the word begins with 'у', by the same euphony rule: 'Він упе́внений.' The unstressed 'е' of the second syllable leans a little toward 'и', as unstressed 'е' always does. The word has the shape of the passive participles in '-ений' of the unit on the passive, such as 'відчи́нений', but it is an ordinary adjective.

Several other words apply familiar rules:

- 'Мо́вний' [ˈmɔwnɪj] and 'словни́к' [slɔwˈnɪk] have 'в' before 'н', said [w], as in 'Петрі́вна'. In every other form of 'словни́к' the stress moves to the ending: 'словника́', 'у словнику́'.
- 'Ві́льно' [ˈʋʲilʲnɔ] has 'в' before a vowel, said [ʋ] and soft before 'і', and the soft sign keeps the 'л' soft before 'н'.
- 'Стиль' [stɪlʲ] ends in a soft 'л', which the soft sign marks. In 'сти́лю' the 'ю' softens the 'л' instead, so no soft sign is written.
- 'Акце́нт' [ɑkˈt͡sɛnt] has 'к' and 'ц' side by side, two separate sounds, and the 'ц' is hard before 'е'. 'Прогре́с' [prɔˈɦrɛs] has the voiced 'г' [ɦ] of the alphabet units. Both are loan words for abstract things and take '-у' in the genitive: 'акце́нту', 'прогре́су'.
- 'Пі́дсумок' [ˈpʲidsumɔk] keeps the 'д' of the prefix 'під-' voiced before the voiceless 'с', as the 'д' of 'від-' does in 'відкла́сти'. Its last 'о' drops when an ending is added: 'пі́дсумку'.
- 'Майбу́тнє' [mɑjˈbutnʲɛ] has three syllables, 'май-бу́т-нє': 'й' closes the first, and 'є' after 'н' softens it and gives [ɛ], as in 'си́нє'. In 'у майбу́тньому' the letters 'ьо' write a soft 'н' plus 'о', as in 'сього́дні'.
- 'По́дяка' [ˈpɔdʲɑkɑ] has a soft 'д' before 'я', as in 'дя́кую', which has the same root.
- 'Бажа́ю у́спіхів' has 'ю' after the vowel 'а', said [ju], and a final 'в' said [w], as in 'Львів'.

examples.target: Я хо́чу ча́сто говори́ти з носіє́м мо́ви.
examples.source: I want to talk often with a native speaker.
examples.source_literal: I want often to-speak with carrier of-language.

examples.target: Тара́с удоскона́лює свою́ англі́йську.
examples.source: Taras is working on his English.

grammar.title: Review: cases, aspect and verbs of motion in a story
grammar.explanation:
A longer text is a chain of choices, and three questions decide most of them. Asking them in turn is a good way to check your own writing and to read a hard sentence.

The first question is asked about every noun: does a preposition stand before it, and if not, what job does it do? Each preposition takes its own case, and some take more than one, each with its own meaning: 'у Ки́єві' (where, the locative) against 'у Ки́їв' (where to, the accusative), and 'з Кана́ди' (from, the genitive) against 'з Окса́ною' (with, the instrumental). Without a preposition the job decides: the subject is in the nominative, the direct object in the accusative, the person who receives or experiences something in the dative, the means or the role in the instrumental, and the owner, a quantity or a thing that is absent in the genitive. Some words bring their own case, which is learned with the word: the genitive after 'нема́є', 'бага́то' and 'боя́тися', the dative with 'подо́батися' and 'тре́ба', the instrumental after 'ста́ти'.

The second question is asked about every verb: is the action presented as a process, a repetition or a plain fact, or as one completed whole with a result? The first view is imperfective, the second perfective. In a story, perfective verbs in a row move the story on, one event after another, while imperfective verbs give the background or say what was going on when something happened: 'Ішо́в дощ, коли́ я приї́хав до Ки́єва.' (It was raining when I arrived in Kyiv.) A question about experience takes the imperfective: 'Ти коли́сь ї́здив до Оде́си?' (Have you ever been to Odesa?)

The third question is asked about every verb of motion: on foot or by vehicle, and in one direction or not? 'Іти́' and 'ї́хати' describe one trip in one direction, now or at a given moment. 'Ходи́ти' and 'ї́здити' describe habits, round trips and movement in general. A prefix adds a direction: on the one-direction verb it makes a perfective ('прийти́', 'приї́хати', 'зайти́'), and on the general verb, or on '-їжджа́ти' for 'ї́хати', the imperfective partner ('прихо́дити', 'приїжджа́ти', 'захо́дити'). 'Піти́' and 'пої́хати' mean setting off.

These sentences from Sam's story show the three questions at work:

- 'Два ро́ки тому́ я приї́хав до Ки́єва.': one arrival by vehicle, completed, so the prefixed perfective 'приї́хати'; 'до' takes the genitive, 'Ки́єва'.
- 'Пе́рший мі́сяць я щодня́ ходи́в на уро́ки.': a trip there and back, repeated, so the general verb 'ходи́ти'; 'на' with the accusative 'уро́ки' says where to; 'пе́рший мі́сяць', in the accusative, says how long.
- 'Одного́ ра́нку я зайшо́в до кафе́ й познайо́мився з Окса́ною.': two events in a row, so two perfectives; 'одного́ ра́нку', one morning, is a genitive of time, and 'з' with the instrumental names the person met.
- 'Ми говори́ли, по́ки Андрі́й вари́в ка́ву.': two processes at the same time, so two imperfectives; 'по́ки' with an imperfective means 'while'.

grammar.title: Review: complex sentences with 'щоб', 'якби́', relative clauses and adverbial participles
grammar.explanation:
A complex sentence joins a main clause to a dependent clause: a clause with its own verb that cannot stand alone, because the word that opens it ties it to the main clause. Earlier units taught four kinds, and a longer text uses all of them. A comma always separates a dependent clause from the main clause.

A clause with 'щоб' says what someone wants, asks for or aims at. With the same subject 'щоб' takes an infinitive: 'Я чита́ю, щоб удоскона́лювати мо́ву.' (I read to improve my language.) With another subject it takes the past form, which here does not mean past time: 'Іри́на Петрі́вна хо́че, щоб Сем писа́в їй листи́.' (Iryna Petrivna wants Sam to write her letters.) 'Щоб' contains the particle 'б' of the conditional, and with the past form it presents the action as wanted, not as done.

A clause with 'якби́' states an unreal condition, one that the speaker presents as not true. Both clauses have the past form, and the main clause adds 'б' or 'би': 'Якби́ ти не приї́хав, ми б не познайо́милися.' (If you hadn't come, we wouldn't have met.) One form serves for the present and the past, so the context decides between 'if you didn't come' and 'if you hadn't come'. A real condition, one that may still be met, takes 'якщо́' and the future: 'Якщо́ ти приї́деш, я тебе́ зустрі́ну.' (If you come, I'll meet you.)

A relative clause describes a noun of the main clause. 'Яки́й' takes its gender and number from that noun and its case from its own job in the clause: 'дру́зі, з яки́ми я говорю́' (the friends I talk with), with the instrumental after 'з'. 'Що' can take the place of 'яки́й', most often as the subject of its clause, but never after a preposition, and 'де', 'куди́' and 'зві́дки' open a clause about a place: 'кафе́, куди́ я ходжу́' (the café I go to).

An adverbial participle adds a second action of the same subject without a second clause. The imperfective form in '-чи' names an action at the same time ('Чита́ючи, я пишу́ нові́ слова́.', As I read, I write down new words), and the perfective form in '-ши' an action completed before ('Поверну́вшись додо́му, Сем подзвони́в ма́мі.', When he got home, Sam called his mom). The one who does it is always the subject of the main verb. It belongs mainly to writing; conversation uses a clause with 'коли́' or two verbs joined by 'і'.

A long sentence often combines several kinds: 'Сем, яки́й два ро́ки жив у Ки́єві, чита́є нови́ни, щоб не забу́ти украї́нську.' (Sam, who lived in Kyiv for two years, reads the news so as not to forget his Ukrainian.)

grammar.title: Review: register, address and the vocative
grammar.explanation:
Register is the level of formality a speaker or a writer chooses for a situation. Ukrainian marks it in several places at once: the pronoun of address, the form of the name, the verb forms, the choice of words and the shape of a written text. A sentence that is correct in one register can sound cold or rude in another.

The pronoun comes first. 'Ти' is for family, friends, children and classmates. 'Ви' is for one person you do not know well, anyone older or senior, a teacher, an official or a customer, and for any group. The verb, the possessive and the imperative follow the pronoun: 'Ти ма́єш ра́цію.' against 'Ви ма́єте ра́цію.'; 'твій' against 'ваш'; 'пиши́' against 'пиші́ть'. When two people who say 'ви' decide to be less formal, the older or more senior one usually suggests it with 'перейти́ на ти', literally 'to cross onto ти': 'Дава́йте пере́йдемо на ти.' (Let's say 'ти' to each other.)

Whenever you call or address someone, the name is in the vocative. Among friends the first name is enough: 'Окса́но!', 'Тара́се!', 'Се́ме!'. In formal speech use 'па́не' or 'па́ні' with the vocative of the first name ('па́не Андрі́ю', 'па́ні Іри́но'), or the first name and the patronymic, both in the vocative ('Іри́но Петрі́вно'). 'Па́ні' never changes; the name after it does. In every other job in the sentence the name takes its ordinary case: 'Це Іри́на Петрі́вна.', 'Я дзвоню́ Іри́ні Петрі́вні.'

A written text has a fixed shape. A formal letter opens with 'Шано́вний' or 'Шано́вна' and the vocative ('Шано́вна Іри́но Петрі́вно!'), writes 'Ви', 'Вам' and 'Ваш' with a capital letter when it addresses one person, states its request with 'Прошу́' and closes with 'З пова́гою,' and the full name. A letter to a friend opens with 'Дороги́й' or 'Дорога́' and the vocative ('Дорога́ Окса́но!'), uses 'ти', and closes with a friendly phrase such as 'До зу́стрічі!' (See you soon!) and the first name.

Speech prefers short, everyday words and constructions, and writing prefers fuller ones:

- 'бо' in speech; 'тому́ що' and 'оскі́льки' in writing
- a clause with 'коли́' in speech ('Коли́ я йшов додо́му, я поба́чив Тара́са.'); an adverbial participle in writing ('Ідучи́ додо́му, я поба́чив Тара́са.')
- the relative word 'що' in speech; 'яки́й' in writing
- verbs in speech ('Зако́н ухвали́ли.'); verbal nouns and the forms in '-но' and '-то' in official writing ('Зако́н ухва́лено.', 'пі́сля ухва́лення зако́ну', after the adoption of the law)
- particles of attitude such as 'ж' and 'ну' in conversation, never in a formal letter

culture.title: Learning Ukrainian among Ukrainians
culture.text:
Many Ukrainians are visibly pleased when a foreigner speaks to them in Ukrainian, even slowly and with mistakes. A learner often hears 'Ви так га́рно гово́рите украї́нською!', literally 'you so beautifully speak by-Ukrainian', meaning 'You speak Ukrainian so well!'. Many Ukrainians also speak English and switch to it to make things easier for a visitor. A learner who wants practice can ask them to stay with Ukrainian: 'Дава́йте говори́ти украї́нською, будь ла́ска.', 'Let's speak Ukrainian, please.'

Conversation meetings for learners are held in libraries, in cafés and online, often free of charge and run by volunteers. Such a meeting is called 'розмо́вний клуб', a conversation club: 'розмо́вний' is the adjective of 'розмо́ва', conversation. Native speakers come to them too, to talk with the learners and to help.

Ukrainians mark November 9 as 'День украї́нської писе́мності та мо́ви', literally 'day of-Ukrainian of-writing and of-language', the Day of Ukrainian Writing and Language. 'Писе́мність' is the written tradition of a language, and 'та' is another word for 'and'. Every year on this day since 2000, Ukrainian Radio has read out a text for a dictation called 'Радіодикта́нт націона́льної є́дності', the radio dictation of national unity. A dictation is a text read aloud for listeners to write down, like the dictation exercises of this course. People across Ukraine and abroad write it at home, at school or at work, and many send in their texts to be checked.

Two phrases of this unit are heard at almost every farewell: 'Бажа́ю у́спіхів!' before an exam, a new job or a journey, and 'Щи́ро дя́кую за все.' to a teacher, a host or a friend.

choices: When a student brings her a present
When native speakers ask her student which Ukrainian city he is from
When a student moves to Ukraine
questions.explanation: If native speakers take the student for someone from a Ukrainian city, his Ukrainian sounds like theirs.

exercises.prompt: Match the Ukrainian with the English
What does 'носі́й мо́ви' say word for word?
exercises.explanation: 'Носі́й' is made from 'носи́ти', to carry, and 'мо́ви' is the genitive of 'мо́ва': 'carrier of language'. The phrase means a native speaker.
'Щи́ро' is the adverb of 'щи́рий', sincere: 'Щи́ро дя́кую.' 'Ві́льно' means fluently, and 'впе́внений' means sure.

choices: Thank you for everything in Lviv!

exercises.hint_source: He speaks Ukrainian without an accent.
exercises.explanation: 'Без' takes the genitive, and 'акце́нт', a loan word for an abstract thing, takes '-у': 'акце́нту'.

exercises.hint_source: This word isn't in the dictionary.
exercises.explanation: 'У' or 'в' for being inside takes the locative. 'Словни́к' takes '-у', as many masculine nouns with a stem in 'к' do, and keeps the stress on the ending: 'у словнику́'.

exercises.hint_source: Oksana is thinking about the future.
exercises.explanation: 'Про' takes the accusative, which for this neuter noun has the same form as the nominative: 'майбу́тнє'. In the locative it keeps its adjective endings: 'у майбу́тньому'.

exercises.audio_target: Я бу́ду сумува́ти за ва́ми всіма́.

exercises.prompt: How is the first letter of 'впе́внений' said?
exercises.explanation: 'В' before a consonant is [w]. In 'впе́внений' both letters 'в' stand before a consonant, so both are [w].

exercises.prompt: Why is the verb written with 'у' in 'Сем удоскона́лює вимо́ву.'?
choices: Because the word before it ends in a consonant
exercises.explanation: By the euphony rule, a word that begins with 'в' before a consonant is written with 'у' after a word that ends in a consonant: 'Я вдоскона́люю вимо́ву.', but 'Сем удоскона́лює вимо́ву.'
When you address someone, the first name and the patronymic are both in the vocative: 'Іри́на' becomes 'Іри́но', as 'Петрі́вна' becomes 'Петрі́вно'.

exercises.prompt: Which line opens a formal letter to Iryna Petrivna?
exercises.explanation: A formal letter opens with 'Шано́вна' and the vocative. 'Приві́т' is said to a friend, and 'До зу́стрічі!' closes a friendly letter.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase closes a formal letter, before the writer's full name?
exercises.explanation: 'З пова́гою', literally 'with respect', closes a formal letter. 'До зу́стрічі!' closes a letter to a friend, and 'Бува́й!' is a spoken goodbye to someone you call 'ти'.
Calling Oksana needs the vocative, 'Окса́но'. 'Щи́ро' usually stands before 'дя́кую'.
'Бажа́ти' takes the person in the dative, 'вам' or 'тобі́', and the thing wished in the genitive, 'у́спіхів'.

exercises.prompt: In the first dialogue, why doesn't Olena come to the café?
choices: She is working at the hospital
exercises.explanation: Taras says: 'Оле́на сього́дні працю́є в лі́карні й прийти́ не мо́же.'

exercises.prompt: In the second dialogue, what does Iryna Petrivna advise Sam to read first?
exercises.explanation: 'Почні́ть з оповіда́нь і нови́н.' Sam dreams of reading 'Лісова́ пі́сня' without a dictionary later.

exercises.prompt: Choose the verb: 'Ко́жного ра́нку Сем ___ до кафе́ Андрі́я.'
exercises.explanation: A trip made every morning, there and back, takes the general verb 'ходи́ти'. 'Ішо́в' describes one trip while it was under way, and 'пішо́в' setting off once.

exercises.prompt: Choose the pair of verbs: 'Сем ___ рома́н ці́лий мі́сяць і вчо́ра наре́шті ___ його́.'
exercises.explanation: A month of reading is a process, so the imperfective 'чита́в'; finishing it yesterday is one completed result, so the perfective 'прочита́в'.

exercises.audio_target: Якби́ ти не приї́хав, ми б не познайо́милися.
choices: If you come, we will meet.
If you hadn't come, we wouldn't have met.

exercises.audio_target: Я впе́внений, що все бу́де до́бре.
choices: I'm afraid it won't go well.
I hope everything will be fine.
I'm sure everything will be fine.

exercises.prompt_target: Іри́на Петрі́вна хо́че, щоб Сем ча́сто ___ їй листи́.
exercises.hint_source: Iryna Petrivna wants Sam to write her letters often.
exercises.explanation: Another subject after 'щоб' takes the past form, here masculine for Sam; it does not mean past time. 'Ча́сто' needs the imperfective 'писа́ти'.
Taras is another subject, so 'щоб' takes the past form: 'прийшо́в' on foot, or 'приї́хав' by vehicle.

exercises.prompt_target: Окса́на, з ___ Сем говори́в украї́нською, до́бре зна́є англі́йську.
exercises.hint_source: Oksana, with whom Sam spoke Ukrainian, knows English well.
exercises.explanation: 'Яки́й' takes the feminine singular from 'Окса́на' and the instrumental from its job in the clause, company after 'з': 'з яко́ю'. The bookish 'котро́ю' is also correct.

exercises.hint_source: Having read the letter, Oksana smiled.
exercises.explanation: The reading is completed before the smile, so the perfective adverbial participle: the masculine past 'прочита́в' plus '-ши'. Its subject is Oksana, the subject of the main verb.

exercises.prompt: Why can't 'Коли́ Сем чита́в, Окса́на пила́ ка́ву.' be said with an adverbial participle?
choices: Because the two actions happen at the same time
Because the two actions have different subjects
exercises.explanation: An adverbial participle always has the subject of the main verb. Here Sam reads and Oksana drinks, so the clause with 'коли́' is needed.
